title: Cause and effect: how one push knocks down a whole line

summary.text: Push the first domino in a line, and the last one falls too, even though you never touched it. Each domino falls because the one before it hits it. What makes something happen is called the cause. What happens is called the effect. In a line of dominoes, every domino is the effect of the one before and the cause of the next. If one gap is too wide, the chain of causes stops there, and the rest of the line stays standing.
summary.art: A child's finger pushing the first of ten matchboxes standing on end in a line on a tiled floor. The first few have fallen, and the rest are still standing.

intro.hook: Stand five books, matchboxes or dominoes on their ends in a row, a little apart. Push only the first one. What happens to the last one? You did not touch it. So what made it fall?
intro.text: Everything that happens is made to happen by something. A push makes a domino fall. Rain makes a puddle. Heat makes ice melt. In this unit you test how far apart dominoes can be and still knock each other down. You send a push through a line of coins and watch only the last coin move. You also find out how people learned that flies come from eggs, and not from rotting meat.
intro.art: Five matchboxes standing on end in a row on the floor. A finger is about to push the first one, and a dotted arrow runs along the row to the last one.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a cause and an effect are, and give examples from my home.
By the end I can show that a push passes along a line of dominoes, from each one to the next.
By the end I can say why a chain stops when one gap is too wide or one domino is missing.
By the end I can show that a push passes through a line of coins and moves the last coin.
By the end I can say that some effects come much later than their cause.
By the end I can say why something that happens first is not always the cause of what comes next.

terms.meaning: A cause is what makes something happen.
terms.example: Your push is the cause of the first domino falling. Heat from the stove is the cause of the milk boiling.
terms.art: A finger pushing a domino, with the word 'cause' and an arrow pointing at the finger.

terms.meaning: An effect is what happens because of a cause.
terms.example: The domino falling is the effect of your push. A puddle is an effect of rain.
terms.art: A domino lying flat on the floor, with the word 'effect' and an arrow pointing at it.

terms.meaning: A chain of causes is when each effect becomes the cause of the next thing, one after another.
terms.example: Dark clouds bring rain. The rain fills the lane with water. The water makes the school van drive slowly. Each one causes the next.
terms.art: Four pictures joined by arrows: a dark cloud, rain falling, a lane full of water, a slow school van.

terms.meaning: Energy is what lets something move or change. A moving thing can pass some of its energy on to what it hits.
terms.example: A falling domino has energy. When it hits the next domino, it passes some energy on, and that one falls too.
terms.art: Two dominoes, one tipping onto the other, with a small star where they touch.

terms.meaning: A gap is the empty space between two things.
terms.example: In the domino test, the gap is the space between one domino and the next.
terms.art: Two dominoes standing up with a space between them, and a small double arrow across the space.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.
terms.example: In the domino test, we change only the gap. We use the same dominoes, the same floor and the same gentle push each time.
terms.art: Three lines of dominoes side by side, the same in every way except for the gaps.

explanations.concept: Cause and effect: every happening is made to happen
explanations.context: This card explains the two words this whole unit is about.
explanations.definition: A cause is what makes something happen. An effect is what happens because of it. The cause always comes first, and the effect comes after.
explanations.description: When you switch on the fan, the curtain starts to move. Switching on the fan is the cause. The moving curtain is the effect. When you drop a steel spoon on a steel plate, the clang is the effect. Every action you do has an effect, even a small one. When you clap, the air shakes and someone in the next room may hear it. Scientists look for causes because, once they know the cause, they can make something happen again, or stop it.
examples: Switching on the fan makes the curtain move.
Stirring sugar into water makes the sugar disappear and the water sweet.
Heat from the gas makes the water in a pot boil.
Rain makes puddles on the road.
explanations.art: A fan turning and a curtain blowing beside it, with an arrow from the fan to the curtain.

explanations.concept: A chain of causes: why the last domino falls
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the domino gap test.
explanations.definition: In a chain of causes, each effect becomes the cause of the next thing. A push can travel a long way like this, but only if every link in the chain passes it on.
explanations.description: In the domino test, your finger pushed only the first domino. As it fell, it hit the second one and passed on some of its energy. The second one fell and hit the third, and so on to the end. When the gap was small, every domino could reach the next one, so the whole line fell. When the gap was as wide as a domino is tall, the first domino lay down without touching the next one. The chain stopped there. Taking one domino out of the middle did the same. The push reached the hole and stopped, so everything after it stayed standing.
examples: A line of dominoes falling one after another
A line of coins passing a push to the last coin
Rain, then a full lane, then a slow school van
A message passed from person to person in a game
explanations.art: A line of dominoes with the first half fallen, then a wide gap, then the second half still standing.

explanations.context: This card explains why we cannot always see the cause and the effect together.
explanations.definition: Some effects happen straight after their cause. Others take hours, days or years to show.
explanations.description: A domino falls at once when it is hit. But many causes take time. When dry chana is soaked in water at night, the seeds slowly drink the water. By morning they are much bigger. A mango seed planted today becomes a tree only after some years. Because the effect comes so late, people sometimes do not notice what caused it. A good scientist keeps asking: what happened before this, maybe a long time before?
examples: Chana soaked tonight is big and soft tomorrow morning.
A seed planted now becomes a tree years later.
Clothes put out in the sun dry after a few hours.
Brushing your teeth every day keeps them healthy for years.
explanations.art: Two bowls of chana side by side: small, hard, dry chana labelled 'night' and big, swollen chana in water labelled 'morning'.

explanations.concept: Something that comes first is not always the cause
explanations.context: This card explains a mistake that everyone makes sometimes.
explanations.definition: Two things can happen one after the other without the first one causing the second. To find the real cause, we test: we change one thing and see what happens.
explanations.description: A rooster crows every morning, and then the Sun rises. Does the rooster make the Sun rise? No. On a day when the rooster stays quiet, the Sun still rises. The rooster crows because morning is coming. So both have the same cause: the Earth turning towards the Sun. This is why scientists do tests. In the domino test, we changed only the gap. Then we knew that the gap was what made the chain stop.
examples: A rooster crows and then the Sun rises, but the rooster does not cause the sunrise.
People carry umbrellas and then it rains, but umbrellas do not cause rain.
You put on your school shoes and then the van comes, but your shoes do not bring the van.
explanations.art: A rooster crowing on a wall as the Sun rises behind the buildings. A second small picture shows the same sunrise with the rooster asleep.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about.
explanations.description: Everything big that we see, like a falling domino, a boiling pot or a puddle, has causes we can find. But some very tiny things are harder. Inside some materials, tiny bits called atoms break apart all by themselves. Nobody can find anything that decides the exact moment one of them breaks. Scientists do not agree about what this means.
examples: A domino falls because it is pushed.
A tiny atom breaks apart at a moment nobody can predict or explain.

perspectives.explanation: For the tiniest things, there may be no cause for the exact moment something happens. It just happens, by chance.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein, and some physicists since
perspectives.explanation: There may be hidden causes that we have not found yet. Einstein wrote in a letter in 1926 that he was sure nature 'does not throw dice'.

perspectives.who: Many thinkers in India and elsewhere
perspectives.explanation: Nothing happens without causes, but every happening has so many causes that nobody can know them all.

explanations.art: On one side, a domino being pushed. On the other, a tiny glowing dot with a question mark beside it.

agreed.text: A push can pass along a line of dominoes, each one knocking over the next.
agreed.evidence: In the domino test, a single gentle push on the first domino made the whole line fall when the gaps were small.

agreed.text: A chain of causes stops where a link is missing or a gap is too wide.
agreed.evidence: In the domino test, the chain stopped when the gap was as wide as a domino is tall, and when one domino was taken out of the middle.

agreed.text: A push can travel through things that hardly move.
agreed.evidence: In the coin chain test, the coins in the middle of the line hardly moved, but the last coin slid away.

agreed.text: Some effects come long after their cause.
agreed.evidence: Dry chana soaked at night only becomes big and soft by the next morning.

agreed.text: Living things do not appear by themselves from rotting food. Flies come from eggs laid by other flies.
agreed.evidence: In 1668, Francesco Redi showed that maggots grew only on meat that flies could reach.

challenging.claim: Maggots and flies grow by themselves out of rotting meat.
challenging.who: Most people in Europe believed this for about two thousand years, and many great thinkers wrote it down.
challenging.for: Rotting meat left out soon had maggots on it, and nobody saw where they came from.
challenging.against: In 1668, Francesco Redi covered some jars of meat with fine cloth. No maggots grew on that meat. Flies had laid their eggs on the cloth instead. Maria Sibylla Merian raised insects from eggs and drew every stage.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that some things have no parents.

challenging.claim: The rooster's crowing makes the Sun rise.
challenging.who: Some old stories say this, and young children often think it.
challenging.for: Every morning the rooster crows first, and then the Sun comes up.
challenging.against: On days when a rooster is ill or quiet, the Sun still rises. Places with no roosters at all still have sunrise.
challenging.context: This card is about mixing up 'comes first' with 'is the cause'.

challenging.claim: A small push can only ever make a small effect.
challenging.for: A gentle push on one domino seems far too small to knock down a whole line.
challenging.against: In the domino test, one gentle push knocked down ten dominoes. A scientist called Lorne Whitehead showed in 1983 that a domino can knock over one about one and a half times bigger than itself.
challenging.context: This card is about whether small causes can have big effects.

challenging.claim: Every effect has just one cause.
challenging.who: We often talk this way, for example 'the wind knocked it over'.
challenging.for: It is easy to name the last thing that happened before the effect.
challenging.against: In the domino test, the last domino fell because of the domino before it, and that one because of the one before it, and so on back to your finger. A cut in any link would have stopped it. So every link was a cause.
challenging.context: This card is about how many causes one effect really has.

big_questions.q: Your finger touched only the first domino. Did your finger knock down the last one, or did the domino next to it?
big_questions.hint: What would have happened if one domino in the middle had been taken away?

big_questions.q: When the gap was too wide, the first domino fell but the second one stayed up. Where did the push go?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the falling domino hit instead.

big_questions.q: Can anything happen with no cause at all?
big_questions.hint: Think of something that seemed to happen all by itself. Was there something before it?

big_questions.q: Everything you do today is the cause of something tomorrow. How far could one small thing you do today reach?
big_questions.hint: Think of the line of dominoes, and how far one push travelled.

big_questions.q: If you follow causes back and back, where does the chain begin?
big_questions.hint: What made the first domino fall? What made you push it? What came before that?

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, most people in Europe believed that small creatures had no parents. They thought maggots grew by themselves out of rotting meat, and caterpillars out of mud and leaves. In 1668, an Italian doctor called Francesco Redi tested this. He put pieces of meat in jars. He left some jars open. He covered others with fine cloth, so air could get in but flies could not. Flies landed on the open meat, and soon it was full of maggots. The covered meat rotted too, but no maggots grew on it. Instead, flies laid their eggs on top of the cloth. So the maggots came from fly eggs, not from the meat. At the same time in Germany, Maria Sibylla Merian was raising caterpillars at home. She fed them leaves and watched them every day. She drew each stage: the egg, the caterpillar, the pupa and the moth. Her book of 1679 showed that every caterpillar hatches from an egg laid by a moth or butterfly.
how_we_found_out.who: Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor, and Maria Sibylla Merian, a German artist and scientist
how_we_found_out.when: Redi's jar test was published in 1668. Merian's first book on caterpillars came out in 1679.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That maggots, caterpillars and other small creatures grow by themselves from rotting meat or mud, with no parents. Redi's covered jars showed that maggots grow only where flies lay eggs, and Merian's drawings showed every stage from egg to moth.
how_we_found_out.art: On the left, three glass jars of meat, one open with flies, one covered with cloth and one sealed. On the right, a woman at a table drawing a caterpillar on a leaf, with a moth and an egg drawn on the same page.

story.title: Meenu and the Coconut That Made the Van Late
story.note: Meenu, Selvi Akka, Fathima and the man on the scooter are made up. Akka means elder sister in Tamil, Kannada and Telugu, and children use it for a young woman they know.
text: Meenu was seven, and she lived in a tall block of flats in Thiruvananthapuram. Every morning, a yellow school van came to the gate at half past seven. Selvi Akka drove it. She knew every road in the city.
One morning, the van did not come. Meenu waited at the gate with her bag. Ten minutes went by. Then twenty. At last the van came round the corner, very slowly.
'Why are you so late, Akka?' asked Meenu, as she climbed in.
'Because of a coconut,' said Selvi Akka.
Meenu laughed. 'A coconut can't make a van late!'
'Wait and see,' said Selvi Akka. She drove out of the gate.
On the main road, the cars were stuck in a long line. Nobody could move. A man on a scooter beside them pressed his horn again and again. 'What is going on?' he shouted. 'Why is nobody moving?'

Selvi Akka leaned out of her window. 'There was a strong wind last night,' she told him. 'The wind shook the coconut trees by the temple. A big coconut fell onto the road. A bus braked hard so as not to hit it. The car behind the bus stopped too. Now every car behind that car has stopped. That is why nobody is moving.'
The man stared at her. 'All this because of one coconut?'
'One coconut, and the wind before it,' said Selvi Akka. 'Each thing made the next thing happen. Honking will not move the coconut.'
The man stopped honking. He even smiled a little.

Meenu looked out of the window. Far ahead, a policewoman was rolling the coconut to the side of the road. Then the bus moved. Then the car behind the bus moved. Then the next car, and the next. The moving went down the line of cars like a wave, until at last it reached their van.
'It is like the dominoes my Amma set up for me,' said Meenu. 'When she pushed the first one, all of them fell, one after another.'
'Just like that,' said Selvi Akka. 'Except now the push is making everyone go, instead of stop.'

Meenu reached school twenty minutes late. The first bell had already rung, and the gate was nearly shut. Standing at the gate, all alone, was a girl Meenu had never seen before. She was holding a new bag very tightly.
'Are you lost?' Meenu asked.
'It's my first day,' said the girl. 'I am Fathima. Our family just moved here from Kozhikode. I don't know which class to go to.'
'You're in Class 2? So am I!' said Meenu. 'Come with me.'
They walked in together. At lunch, they shared Meenu's idiyappam and Fathima's banana chips. By the end of the day, they were friends.
That evening, Meenu sat with Amma on the balcony. She told her about the coconut, the bus, the cars and the man on the scooter.

'If the wind had not blown,' said Meenu slowly, 'the coconut would not have fallen. If the coconut had not fallen, the van would not have been late. If the van had not been late, I would not have been at the gate when Fathima was there. And then she would not be my friend.'
Amma nodded. 'So what caused your new friend?'
Meenu thought hard. 'The wind? The coconut? Selvi Akka? Fathima's family moving here? Me, for asking if she was lost?' She frowned. 'All of them?'
'All of them,' said Amma. 'And many more things that we will never know about.'
Meenu looked down at the road below. A gust of wind was shaking the coconut trees. She wondered what it would make happen tomorrow.
story.epiphany: One coconut falling in the night was the start of a long chain of causes. Each thing that happened made the next one happen, and the chain reached all the way to Meenu's new friend.
ask: Why were all the cars stuck, when only the bus had to stop for the coconut?
When the coconut was moved, the cars did not all start at once. Why did they start one after another?
Meenu found many causes for her new friendship. Can you think of one more?
What small thing happened to you today that might cause something tomorrow?

Meenu and Fathima walking through a school gate together.

experiments.title: The Domino Gap Test: how far apart can they be?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stand ten dominoes in a line and push the first one. You try three different gaps between them, and count how many fall each time.
experiments.question: How far apart can dominoes stand and still knock each other down, all the way to the end of the line?
experiments.predict: We will try three gaps: one finger wide, half a domino tall, and one whole domino tall. Which gaps will make all ten dominoes fall? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We change only the gap. We use the same ten dominoes on the same floor each time. We give the first domino the same gentle push with one finger. We switch off the fan, because moving air can knock over light dominoes. We try each gap twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: First try: how many fell (out of 10)?
Second try: how many fell (out of 10)?

materials.item: 10 dominoes, or 10 empty matchboxes, or 10 wooden building blocks that are all the same size
one strip of paper, a little longer than a domino
a flat, hard floor or a big table with no cloth on it

experiments.safety: If you use matchboxes, take all the matches out first. A grown-up keeps the matches away from children.

schedule.what: Make the gap strip. Stand up ten dominoes three times, with three different gaps. Push the first one and count how many fall.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then draw the line of dominoes for the widest gap, showing which ones fell and which stayed up.

setup.art: The same paper strip folded in half, with the fold marked.
setup.caption: 2. Fold it in half to find half a domino's height.

setup.art: Ten matchboxes standing on end in a straight line on a tiled floor, each one a finger's width from the next.
setup.caption: 3. Stand ten dominoes in a line, the same gap apart.

setup.art: A child's finger gently pushing the first matchbox, and the first three falling onto each other.
setup.caption: 4. Push the first one gently. Count how many fall.

flow.context: This is the first step of the domino gap test. You make a strip of paper to measure the gaps.
flow.do: 1. Stand one domino on its short end on the paper strip. 2. Your child marks the strip level with the top of the domino. 3. Cut the strip at the mark. 4. Fold it in half and mark the fold.
flow.say: This strip is exactly as long as a domino is tall. Folded in half, it shows half a domino's height. We will use it to set the gaps.
flow.kid: Stand a domino on the paper. Mark how tall it is. Cut the paper there. Fold it in half.
flow.parent: Measuring with the strip means the test works with any dominoes, matchboxes or blocks, whatever their size.

flow.context: In this step of the domino gap test, you guess what will happen.
flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan. 2. Show your child the three gaps: one finger, half the strip and the whole strip. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: We will try three gaps. One finger wide. Half a domino tall. One whole domino tall. For which gaps will all ten fall? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are three gaps to try. Which gaps will make all ten fall? Why?

ask.q: Which gaps will make all ten dominoes fall? Why?
good: The small gaps, because each domino can reach the next one.
The big gap, because the domino falls harder from further away.
All of them, because a push always goes on.

flow.parent: Write down your child's guess and their reason. Do not say who is right. Many children think a bigger gap gives a harder hit.

flow.context: In this step of the domino gap test, you try the smallest gap: one finger wide.
flow.do: 1. Your child stands ten dominoes in a straight line, one finger apart. 2. Start at the far end, so a slip knocks over only a few. 3. Push the first domino gently with one finger. 4. Count how many fell. 5. Do it once more.
flow.say: Put one finger between each domino and the next. Now give the first one a gentle push. Don't push hard. How many fell?
flow.kid: Stand ten dominoes in a line, one finger apart. Push the first one gently. Count how many fall.
flow.parent: If some fall while your child is setting them up, that is normal. Stand them up again. With a one-finger gap, all ten usually fall.

flow.context: In this step of the domino gap test, you try a gap of half a domino's height.
flow.do: 1. Stand the ten dominoes again, using the half strip to set each gap. 2. Push the first one gently. 3. Count how many fell. 4. Do it once more.
flow.say: Now use the half strip for each gap. The gaps are bigger this time. Will they all fall? Push the first one gently.
flow.kid: Use the half strip to make each gap. Push the first one. Count how many fall.
flow.parent: With half a domino's height as the gap, all ten usually still fall. Each one hits the next one high up, near the top.

flow.context: In this step of the domino gap test, you try the widest gap: as wide as a domino is tall.
flow.do: 1. Stand the ten dominoes again, using the whole strip to set each gap. 2. Push the first one gently. 3. Watch where the first domino lands. 4. Count how many fell. 5. Do it once more.
flow.say: Now each gap is as wide as a domino is tall. Push the first one. Watch where it lands. How many fell this time?
flow.kid: Make each gap as wide as the whole strip. Push the first one. Watch where it lands.

ask.q: Where did the first domino land? Did it touch the second one?
good: It lay down flat and just reached the bottom of the next one.
It did not reach the next one, so that one stayed up.

flow.parent: Usually only the first one falls. Lying flat, it just reaches the bottom of the next domino, too low to tip it. If your dominoes slide on a smooth floor, try a rough tile or a table.

flow.context: This is the last step of the domino gap test. You take one domino out and say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Stand the line again with the half-strip gaps. 2. Take out the fifth domino. 3. Push the first one and count how many fall. 4. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 5. Then read the card on why the last domino falls.
flow.say: This time we take one domino out of the middle. What will happen? Push. How many fell? Why do you think the chain stopped where it did?
flow.kid: Take out the fifth domino. Push the first one. Where does the chain stop? Why?

good: The fourth domino had nothing to hit.
There was a big hole, so the push could not get across.
Each domino only falls if the one before it hits it.

check.q: In the domino test, why did the last domino fall when the gaps were small?
options: The domino next to it hit it
check.why: Your finger touched only the first domino. Each domino was knocked over by the one before it. The fan was off, so it was not the wind.

flow.parent: Four dominoes fall, then the chain stops at the hole. Let your child explain it before you read the card. A strong answer says that each domino falls only when the one before it hits it.

experiments.title: The Coin Chain: which coin moves?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put coins in a line, touching each other. You slide one more coin into the end of the line, and watch which coin moves away.
experiments.question: If you slide a coin into one end of a line of coins, which coin will move away?
experiments.predict: When the sliding coin hits the line, which coin will move? The first one, the middle ones, the last one, or all of them? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the coins are the same kind, so they are the same size and weight. They touch each other in a straight line. We slide the coin the same way each time, on the same smooth surface. We try each test three times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 7 coins that are all the same kind, for example seven 5-rupee coins
a carrom board, or a smooth table, or a smooth tiled floor
a ruler or a straight book edge, to line the coins up

schedule.what: Line up five coins touching. Slide one coin into the end, then two coins. Watch which coins move away.

experiments.record: Draw the line of coins before and after each test. Draw an arrow on each coin that moved.

setup.caption: 1. Line up five coins so they touch.

setup.art: A finger flicking a sixth coin along the board towards the end of the line.
setup.caption: 2. Slide one coin into the end of the line.

flow.context: This is the first step of the coin chain test. You line up the coins and guess.
flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler on the board. 2. Your child puts five coins along its edge, all touching. 3. Take the ruler away gently. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: These five coins are all touching. We will slide another coin into this end. Which coin will move away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put five coins in a line, touching. Which coin will move when another coin hits? Why?

ask.q: Which coin will move away when the sliding coin hits?
good: The first coin, because it gets hit.
All of them, because they all get pushed.
The last coin, because the push goes along.

flow.parent: Write down your child's guess and reason. Most children guess the first coin, or all of them.

flow.context: In this step of the coin chain test, you slide one coin into the line.
flow.do: 1. Put a sixth coin about one hand-length from the end of the line, in a straight line with it. 2. Your child flicks it with a finger so it slides straight into the line. 3. Watch which coin moves. 4. Set up again and do it three times.
flow.say: Flick this coin so it slides straight into the end of the line. Watch carefully. Which coin moved?
flow.kid: Flick the coin into the line. Watch closely. Which coin moved away?

ask.q: Which coin moved? What did the middle coins do?
good: The last coin slid away.
The middle coins hardly moved at all.

flow.parent: On a smooth board, the coin you flick stops, the middle coins hardly move, and the last coin slides away. If all the coins scatter, the line was not straight or the coins were not touching. Set them up again.

flow.context: In this step of the coin chain test, you slide two coins in at once.
flow.do: 1. Set up the line of five again. 2. Put two coins touching each other, one hand-length away. 3. Your child flicks the back coin, so both slide into the line together. 4. Watch how many coins move away at the far end.
flow.say: This time, two coins hit the line together. How many coins will move away at the other end? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two coins hit the line together. How many move away at the end?
flow.parent: Usually two coins slide away at the far end. If only one moves, check that the two coins were touching as they slid. Try again.

flow.context: This is the last step of the coin chain test. You say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Then read the card on why the last domino falls.
flow.say: The middle coins hardly moved. But the last coin flew off. How did the push get to the end?
flow.kid: The middle coins hardly moved. How did the push get to the end coin?

ask.q: How did the push get from the first coin to the last coin?
good: Each coin pushed the next one.
The push went through the coins, like through dominoes.
The coins passed it on without moving much.

flow.parent: The push travels through the coins as a quick squeeze from one to the next. The middle coins pass it on and stay almost still. The last coin has nothing to pass it to, so it moves away.

activities.title: Do It and See: six actions, six effects
activities.context: In this activity you do six small actions around the house. After each one, you say what happened because of it.

materials.item: a steel spoon and a steel plate
a tumbler of water, a spoon and a little sugar
a strip of paper or a light cloth
a steel tumbler or a small mirror

schedule.what: Do six actions and say the effect of each one. Then try to find an action with no effect.

activities.record: Draw one action and its effect, with an arrow from the action to the effect.

setup.art: A child dropping a steel spoon onto a steel plate, with lines showing the clang.
setup.caption: 1. Do an action.

setup.art: A child breathing onto a shiny steel tumbler, and a cloudy patch on the steel.
setup.caption: 2. Say what happened because of it.

flow.do: 1. Your child drops the spoon onto the plate. 2. Holds the paper strip in front of the fan and switches the fan on. 3. Stirs a spoon of sugar into the water and tastes it. 4. Breathes on the steel tumbler. 5. Claps once. 6. Switches the light off and on.
flow.say: Do this, and tell me what happened because of it. What you did is called the cause. What happened is called the effect.
flow.kid: Do each action. Then say what happened. What you did is the cause. What happened is the effect.

ask.q: What was the effect of breathing on the tumbler?
good: The steel went cloudy.
A misty patch came on it, and then it went away.

flow.parent: Your breath is warm and wet. The cold steel turns some of that water into tiny drops, so it looks cloudy.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to find an action that has no effect at all. 2. Talk about each one they try.
flow.say: Can you find an action that has no effect at all? Try something. Now, did anything change, even a tiny bit?
flow.kid: Try to find an action with no effect at all. Did anything change, even a little?

ask.q: Was there an action with no effect at all?
good: No. Even blinking moves the air a tiny bit.
Waving my hand moved the air.
When I whispered, Amma heard me.

flow.parent: Any action changes something, even if only a little: it moves air, makes a sound or warms what you touch. Let your child test their ideas. There is no need to settle it now.

activities.title: Cause Detectives: what made this happen?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up leaves four effects around the house. You find each one and work out what caused it, using clues.

materials.item: a little water, a book, a few crumbs of biscuit and a chappal

schedule.what: Find four effects around the house and work out the cause of each, using clues.

activities.record: For each effect, draw it and write one word for its cause.

setup.art: A small puddle of water on a kitchen floor beside a dripping tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Find an effect.

setup.art: A girl with a paper magnifying glass looking at biscuit crumbs on a plate.
setup.caption: 2. Look for clues to the cause.

flow.do: 1. Before you start, without your child seeing, spill a little water near a tumbler. 2. Leave a book on the floor near a table edge. 3. Leave biscuit crumbs on a plate. 4. Put one chappal upside down by the door.
flow.say: Something happened in four places in our home. Your job is to find out what caused each one. Look for clues.
flow.kid: Four things happened at home. Find them. Look for clues. What caused each one?
flow.parent: Choose effects with clear clues. The wet tumbler is a clue for the water. The table edge is a clue for the book.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds each effect. 2. For each one, ask the questions below.
flow.say: What do you think caused this? What clue tells you? Could anything else have caused it?
flow.kid: What caused this? What clue tells you? Could it be something else?

ask.q: What caused the crumbs on the plate? How do you know?
good: Someone ate a biscuit there, because the crumbs are biscuit crumbs.
A biscuit broke on the plate.

flow.parent: Praise the clue more than the answer. 'The tumbler is wet on the outside' is real evidence. Some effects have more than one possible cause, and that is a good thing to notice.

flow.do: 1. Switch on a light just as your child walks into the room. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: The light came on just as you walked in. Did your walking in make the light come on?
flow.kid: The light came on as you walked in. Did you make it come on?

ask.q: Did walking in make the light come on?
good: No, you pressed the switch.
It only happened at the same time.

flow.parent: This shows that two things can happen together, or one after the other, without one causing the other.

activities.title: The Ant Message Chain
activities.context: In this activity you put a drop of sugar water where ants walk. You watch how one ant finding the sugar leads to many ants coming. This works if ants visit your kitchen or balcony.

materials.item: a few drops of sugar water

schedule.what: Put sugar water near an ant path. Look at it three times, 10 minutes apart. Count the ants.

activities.record: Draw the paper each time you look, with a dot for each ant. Write the time and the number of ants.

setup.art: A drop of sugar water on a small square of paper on a kitchen counter, near a line of tiny ants walking along the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Put a drop of sugar water near where ants walk.

setup.art: The same paper later, with many small ants gathered round the drop and a line of ants coming to it.
setup.caption: 2. Look again later. Count the ants.

flow.do: 1. Find a place where you have seen ants, such as a kitchen counter, a window sill or a balcony. 2. Put a drop of sugar water on the paper there. 3. Count the ants on the paper now.
flow.say: Ants walk here sometimes. Let's put a drop of sugar water on this paper and count the ants. Then we wait.
flow.kid: Put a drop of sugar water on the paper, near the ants. Count the ants now.
flow.parent: If no ants come within an hour, try again near a different wall or window. Some flats have no ants at all, and then this activity is for another day.

flow.do: 1. Look again and count the ants. 2. Look once more ten minutes after that.
flow.say: How many ants are there now? Where are they coming from? Do they walk in a line?
flow.kid: Count the ants now. Are they walking in a line?

ask.q: How did so many ants know where the sugar was?
good: The first ant told the others.
They followed each other's path.
They smelled it.

flow.parent: Many kinds of ants leave a trail of smell on the way home from food. Other ants smell the trail and follow it, so one ant's find brings many ants.

flow.do: 1. Talk about the chain together. 2. Afterwards, move the paper outside or wipe the sugar away, without hurting the ants.
flow.say: First the sugar. Then one ant found the sugar. Then she left a smell trail. Then many ants came. What started the chain?
flow.kid: One ant found the sugar. Then many came. What started the chain?
flow.parent: Ants sense, decide and tell each other where food is. Some scientists call the trail an automatic response. Either way, one ant's find was the cause of all the others coming.

games.title: Chain Builder: a card game of causes
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or 1 player building the chains alone
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows something that happens. You build chains of causes, where each card makes the next one happen.

items.f: Dark clouds blow in from the sea over Kochi.
Water fills the lane outside the flats.
The school van has to drive very slowly.
Asha's teacher waits for her before starting the story.
Amma lights the gas under the tawa.
Amma pours dosa batter onto the hot tawa.
The batter cooks and turns crisp and brown.
The smell of dosa fills the flat.
Thatha comes into the kitchen, hungry.
A ripe mango falls from the tree.
A squirrel eats the mango and leaves the seed.
Rain soaks the seed lying in the soil.
The seed sends out a root and a shoot.
Years later, a young mango tree stands there.
The young tree grows ripe mangoes.
items.b: Mango chain, card 6 of 6. This leads back to card 1, so the chain is a loop.

rules: Cut out the 18 cards. Find the three cards that say 'card 1' on the back. Lay them face up in a row. These start the three chains.
Shuffle the other 15 cards. Give each player 4 cards. Put the rest face down in a pile.
On your turn, put down one card that can come next in any chain. Say the chain out loud with 'so': 'The tawa gets hot, so Amma pours the batter.'
The other players turn your card over. If the back shows the right chain and the right number, you keep it there. If not, take it back.
If you cannot put down a card, take one from the pile.
The first player with no cards left wins. Playing alone, build all three chains, then check the backs.

setup.art: Three cards in a row on a floor: dark clouds, a gas flame under a tawa, and a mango falling, with small cards in two children's hands.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three start cards. Deal 4 cards each.

setup.art: A girl laying a card that shows a hot tawa next to the gas flame card, saying 'so'.
setup.caption: 2. Put down a card that comes next. Say the chain with 'so'.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Lay out the three start cards. 3. Read the rules out loud.
flow.say: Each card is something that happens. You add a card that the last card makes happen. Then you say it with 'so', to show the cause and the effect.
flow.kid: Add a card that the last card makes happen. Say it with 'so'.

flow.do: 1. Take turns adding cards. 2. Say each new link out loud with 'so'. 3. Check the back of each card.
flow.say: The rain falls all afternoon, so what happens next? Which card shows the effect?
flow.kid: Find the card that comes next. Say the link with 'so'.

ask.q: Why can't 'Asha reaches school late' come straight after 'Dark clouds blow in'?
good: Something has to happen in between.
The clouds don't make her late by themselves. The rain and the water in the lane do.

flow.parent: If a player's card could fit in a sensible way, even if the back says otherwise, let them explain it. A good reason counts.

flow.do: 1. When all the chains are finished, look at the mango chain. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the mango chain. What does the last card lead to?
flow.kid: Look at the last mango card. What does it lead to next?

ask.q: What does the last mango card lead to?
good: A ripe mango falls again, so the chain starts again.
It goes round in a circle.

check.q: In the dosa chain, what is the cause of the tawa getting hot?
check.why: The gas flame heats the tawa. The smell and Thatha coming in happen later, so they are effects, not the cause.

flow.parent: A chain that comes back to the start is called a loop. Many chains in nature are loops: mango, seed, tree, mango.

games.title: Pass the Push: a human chain game
games.players: 3 or more players, and one person to time
games.context: This is a game you play with your bodies. Players stand in a line. Each one pats the next person's shoulder only when they feel a pat. You time how long the pat takes to reach the end.

printables.title: Pass the Push timing sheet
items: Try 1, eyes open: seconds from the first pat to the last person's hand going up
Try 5, one person in the middle steps out: did the pat reach the end?

rules: Stand in a line, one behind the other, each facing the back of the person in front.
The timer says 'Go' and pats the shoulder of the person at the back of the line.
When you feel a pat, pat the shoulder of the person in front of you. Do not pat before you feel it.
The person at the front puts a hand up as soon as they feel the pat. The timer stops the phone's stopwatch.
Write the time on the sheet. Try again with eyes closed.
Last, one person in the middle steps out and does not pat. Does the pat still reach the front?

setup.art: Three family members standing in a line in a living room, one behind the other, and a girl with a phone stopwatch at the back.
setup.caption: 1. Stand in a line. The timer pats the last person.

setup.art: A grandmother patting the shoulder of a boy in front of her, who is about to pat the girl in front of him.
setup.caption: 2. When you feel a pat, pass it on.

flow.do: 1. Stand in a line. 2. Read the rules out loud. 3. Have one practice try.
flow.say: You can only pat when you feel a pat. Each person is one domino. Let's see how fast the push can travel.
flow.kid: Pat the person in front only when you feel a pat.

flow.do: 1. Do two tries with eyes open and two with eyes closed. 2. Write each time on the sheet.
flow.say: How many seconds did it take? Will it be faster or slower with eyes closed? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many seconds did it take? Try with eyes closed. Is it faster or slower?

ask.q: Why does the pat take some time to get to the front?
good: Each person needs a moment to feel it and pat.
It has to go through every person, one at a time.

flow.parent: Each person takes a short moment to feel the pat and pass it on. More people in the line means a longer time.

flow.do: 1. One person in the middle steps out to the side and does not pat. 2. Play once more.
flow.say: Now one link is missing. Will the pat still reach the front?
flow.kid: One person steps out. Does the pat still get to the front?

good: The person who stepped out did not pass it on.
There was a missing link, like the missing domino.

flow.parent: The pat stops at the gap, just like the domino line with one domino taken out.

projects.title: Tonight's Cause, Tomorrow's Effect: soaking chana
projects.context: In this project you soak dry chana in water at night. You measure a line of chana before and after, to see an effect that takes all night to happen.

materials.item: a small handful of dry chana (chickpeas), white or black
a ruler, or a strip of paper to mark on

schedule.what: Line up ten dry chana and measure the line. Soak them in water overnight.
Line up the same ten chana and measure again. Compare.

projects.record: Write how long the line of ten chana was at night and in the morning. Draw one chana before and after, the right sizes.

setup.art: Ten dry chana in a touching line along a ruler, with the length marked.
setup.caption: 1. At night, line up ten dry chana and measure.

setup.art: Ten swollen chana in a line along the same ruler, reaching much further.
setup.caption: 2. In the morning, line them up again.

flow.do: 1. Your child lines up ten dry chana, touching, along a ruler. 2. Write down the length. 3. Put them in a bowl with plenty of water. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: We put these chana in water tonight. What will they look like in the morning? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Line up ten chana. Measure the line. Put them in water. What will happen by morning? Why?

ask.q: What will the chana look like in the morning? Why?
good: Bigger, because they drink the water.
Softer, because water goes inside.
The same, because they are hard.

flow.parent: Many homes soak chana overnight before cooking. Use plenty of water, at least three times as much as the chana.

flow.do: 1. Take out the same ten chana. 2. Your child lines them up along the ruler again. 3. Compare the two lengths. 4. Look at how much water is left in the bowl.
flow.say: How long is the line now? Is there less water in the bowl? Where did the water go? When did we cause this?
flow.kid: Measure the line again. Is it longer? Where did the water go?

ask.q: The cause happened last night. Why could we only see the effect this morning?
good: The chana drink the water slowly.
It takes many hours for water to get inside.

flow.parent: The line of ten is usually much longer in the morning, because the seeds have soaked up water. Cook the chana afterwards, so nothing is wasted.

challenges.title: The Chain Reaction Machine: ring a bell with one push
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a chain of at least four causes. The last effect must ring a steel bowl or drop a coin into a cup.
challenges.problem: Make a machine where one gentle push starts a chain of at least four causes, and the last one rings a steel bowl or drops a coin into a cup.
constraints: You may touch only the first part, once.
There must be at least four steps, each causing the next.
Use things from home, and put everything back afterwards.
materials: books, to make ramps and walls
a ruler or a strip of cardboard
a marble, a small ball or a round lemon
a steel bowl or a steel tumbler
a coin and a paper cup
general: A line of dominoes falls onto a ruler lying across a pencil, like a see-saw. The other end of the ruler flips up and hits the steel bowl.
The last domino pushes a marble down a ramp made from a book. The marble rolls into a steel tumbler and rings it.
creative: Make the dominoes grow in size, from a matchbox to a small book. Each one can knock over one a little bigger than itself.
Make the marble knock a coin off the edge of a table into a cup.
Add a turn in the domino line, around a corner of a book.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your machine first, with an arrow from each cause to its effect. Then build it. If it stops, find the link that did not pass the push on, fix it, and try again.

setup.art: A drawing on paper of a domino line, a ramp and a steel bowl, with arrows from one to the next.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your machine with arrows from cause to effect.

setup.art: A child's machine on the floor: matchboxes leading to a book ramp, with a lemon ready to roll down into a steel bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Build it. Push the first part once.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Your child draws a plan with arrows.
flow.say: One push has to start at least four causes in a row. The last one must ring the bowl. Draw your plan first. Put an arrow from each cause to its effect.
flow.kid: Draw your machine. Draw an arrow from each cause to its effect.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the machine. 2. Test it. 3. When it stops, look for the link that failed. 4. Fix it and try again.
flow.say: Where did the chain stop? Which link did not pass the push on? What could you change there?
flow.kid: Push the first part. Where did it stop? Fix that link and try again.
flow.parent: Chains nearly always fail a few times. Help your child find the exact link that failed, rather than starting again from scratch.

flow.do: 1. Run the finished machine. 2. Your child names each cause and effect in order.
flow.say: Tell me the chain, from the first push to the ring. Use 'so' between each step.
flow.kid: Say your chain from start to end. Use 'so' between each step.

ask.q: Which link was the hardest to get right? Why?
good: The ramp, because the marble rolled off the side.
The dominoes, because the gap was too big.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: what happens because of a cause
each effect causes the next thing
the empty space between two things
items.why: These are the words the child needs to talk about the domino test. A cause makes something happen, and the effect is what happens.

items.p: In the domino test, what happened when each gap was as wide as a domino is tall?
items.why: The first domino fell when it was pushed, but it lay down without tipping the next one. Choosing 'all ten fell' means thinking a bigger gap gives a harder hit. The test shows the domino cannot reach.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: Each pair below is a cause and its effect. Sort each one into 'cause' or 'effect'.
items: a push on the first domino
items.why: In each pair, the cause comes first and makes the effect happen. The fan moves the curtain, the heat boils the water, the push tips the domino.

items.p: Draw your domino line with the widest gap, after you pushed the first one. Show which dominoes fell and which stayed standing.
items.a: One domino lying flat, its top just reaching the bottom of the next one, and nine dominoes still standing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the fallen domino not reaching high enough to tip the next one. That is the evidence for why the chain stopped.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: In the domino test, your finger touched every domino in the line.
items.why: False. Your finger touched only the first domino. Each of the others was knocked over by the domino before it.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: when we took the fifth domino out, why did the chain stop?
items.a: The fourth domino had nothing to hit, so the push could not get past the hole.
items.why: A strong answer says that each domino falls only when the one before it hits it. Saying 'because it was broken' does not say which link was missing.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: Put this chain of causes in order.
items: Dark clouds come over the city
items.why: Each one causes the next. The clouds bring rain, the rain fills the lane, and the water makes the van go slowly.

items.p: Kavya stood up 10 dominoes with the widest gap. When she pushed, only 1 fell. How many stayed standing?
items.why: 10 take away 1 is 9. Nine dominoes stayed standing, because the first one could not reach the second.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 2, and her brother Arjun watch the last domino fall.

views.says: My finger knocked down the last domino, because I started the push.
The domino next to it knocked it down. Your finger never touched it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, then sees the other side. For example: Arjun is right that the ninth domino hit the last one. Meenakshi is right that without her push, nothing would have fallen.
items.why: Both are partly right. The last domino's nearest cause was its neighbour. But the push started with the finger. Every link in a chain is a cause.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: What makes something happen is called the ____.
items.why: The cause comes first and makes something happen. What happens is the effect.

items.p: In the coin chain test, one coin slid into the line. Which coin moved away?
opts: The first coin in the line
items.why: The push travelled through the coins, and only the last one moved away. Choosing 'the first coin' makes sense, because it was hit. But it passed the push on instead of moving.
items.context: This question is about the coin chain test. You put coins in a touching line and slid one more coin into the end.

items.p: The middle coins hardly moved. So how did the push get to the last coin?
items.a: Each coin pushed on the next one, and passed the push along without moving much. The last coin had nothing to pass it to, so it moved away.
items.why: A strong answer says that each coin passed the push to the next. Saying 'it jumped over' misses that the coins touched and passed it on.
items.context: This question is about the coin chain test. You put coins in a touching line and slid one more coin into the end.

items.p: Draw the coin line before and after you slid two coins in together. Put an arrow on each coin that moved away.
items.a: A line of five coins with two coins coming in at one end, and then two coins sliding away from the far end.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same number of coins leaving as came in, with the middle coins staying in place.
items.context: This question is about the coin chain test. You put coins in a touching line and slid one more coin into the end.

items.p: In three of these, the first thing causes the second. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Switching on the fan, then the curtain moves
The rooster crows, then the Sun rises
Stirring in sugar, then the water tastes sweet
Lighting the gas, then the tawa gets hot
items.why: The rooster crows before sunrise, but the Sun would rise anyway. Both happen because morning is coming. In the other three, the first thing really causes the second.

items.p: If one thing happens just before another, the first thing must be its cause.
items.why: False. A rooster crows before sunrise, but does not make the Sun rise. To find a real cause, we test by changing one thing.

items.p: Meenu, a girl in Class 2, made a new friend after her school van was late because a coconut fell on the road. Her cousins Revathi and Joel talk about it.

views.says: The coconut caused the friendship. Without it, the van would not have been late.
Meenu caused it. She chose to talk to the new girl at the gate.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason and sees the other side. For example: Joel is right that Meenu chose to speak. Revathi is right that Meenu would not have been there without the coconut.
items.why: Both are real causes. A happening usually has many causes, some that just happen and some that people choose.

items.p: Soaked overnight in water, dry chana become ____ by the morning.
items.why: The chana seeds soak up water through the night. The effect takes hours to show.
items.context: This question is about soaking chana. You measured a line of ten dry chana at night, soaked them, and measured them again in the morning.

items.p: Label the two pictures: write 'cause' under one and 'effect' under the other.
a: a rain cloud pouring rain: cause
a puddle on the road: effect
items.why: The rain comes first and makes the puddle. So the rain is the cause, and the puddle is the effect.
items.art: Two pictures side by side with an arrow between them: a cloud raining, and a puddle on a road. Under each is an empty line.

items.p: Before soaking, Kavya's line of 10 chana was 8 centimetres long. In the morning, it was 12 centimetres long. How much longer was it?
items.why: 12 take away 8 is 4. The line was 4 centimetres longer, because each chana had soaked up water.
items.context: This question is about soaking chana. You measured a line of ten dry chana at night, soaked them, and measured them again in the morning.

items.p: Why did the chain stop when the gap was as wide as a domino is tall?
opts: The falling domino could not reach high enough on the next one
items.why: Lying flat, the first domino just reached the bottom of the next one, which is too low to tip it. The dominoes were the same as in the other tests, so weight was not the reason.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: Does the floor change how well a domino chain works? Say how you would test it, and what you would keep the same.
items.a: Set up the same ten dominoes with the same gap, first on a smooth tile and then on a mat. Push the same way. Keep the dominoes, the gap and the push the same, and change only the floor.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the floor and keeps everything else the same, so any difference must be caused by the floor.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 2, and her grandmother watch a domino line fall.

views.says: I saw each domino push the next one. I saw the cause.
I saw one domino move, and then the next one move. I never saw the push itself, only one thing after another.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For example: Nila is right that the dominoes touched and pushed. Her grandmother is right that what our eyes see is one movement after another.
items.why: This is a real question that thinkers have argued about. The Scottish thinker David Hume said, in 1748, that we never see a cause itself, only one thing following another.

items.p: Draw a plan for a machine where one push starts four causes in a row, and the last one rings a steel bowl. Put an arrow from each cause to its effect.
items.a: A drawing with at least four parts, such as dominoes, a ruler see-saw, a rolling marble and a steel bowl, each joined by an arrow.
items.why: A strong plan has every link able to reach the next one. Each arrow shows which thing makes the next one happen.

items.p: In 1668, Francesco Redi put meat in jars. Some were open and some were covered with fine cloth. What grew on the covered meat?
items.why: Flies could not reach the covered meat, so no maggots grew on it. This showed that maggots come from fly eggs, not from the meat itself.

items.p: Put the ant message chain in order.
items: A drop of sugar water is put near the ants' path
She leaves a smell trail on her way home
Many ants follow the trail to the sugar
items.why: The sugar comes first. The first ant's find, and her smell trail, cause many other ants to come.

items.p: A falling domino can knock over a domino that is a little bigger than itself.
items.why: True. In 1983, a scientist called Lorne Whitehead showed that a domino can knock over one about one and a half times its size. So a chain of growing dominoes can end with a very big one.

items.p: Sort these effects: does each one come straight after its cause, or much later?
items: a clang when a spoon hits a plate
a mango seed growing into a tree
a curtain moving when the fan is on
wet clothes drying in the sun
items.why: Some effects happen in a moment. Others take hours or years. A late effect is easy to miss, so we keep asking what happened before.

items.p: The domino line and the coin line are different. Say one way they are the same.
items.a: In both, a push went from one thing to the next, all the way to the end. Only the first one was touched.
items.why: A strong answer names the chain: each part passing the push to the next. Saying 'they both fell' is not true, because the coins slid.

items.p: A chain of causes stops where one ____ is missing.
items.why: Each link passes the push to the next. When one is missing, as when we took out the fifth domino, the push stops there.
items.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.

items.p: Which of these chains is broken, so the effect at the end will not happen?
opts: Push, domino, a wide empty gap, domino, bell
Pat, person, person, person, hand goes up
items.why: The wide empty gap means the domino before it has nothing to hit. In the other two, every link can reach the next.

quiz.why: A cause makes something happen. The effect is what happens because of it.

quiz.p: You switch on the fan, and the curtain moves. What is the effect?
quiz.why: The curtain moving is what happens because of the fan. Switching on the fan is the cause.

quiz.p: Ten dominoes stand one finger apart. You push only the first one. What usually happens?
opts: All ten fall, one after another
They all fall at the same moment
quiz.why: Each domino hits the next one, so they fall one after another. They do not fall together, because the push takes a moment to travel down the line.

quiz.p: Which domino knocks over the last domino in a line?
quiz.why: Each domino is knocked over by its neighbour. The first one starts the chain, but it never touches the last one.

quiz.p: A domino in the middle of the line is taken away. What happens when you push the first one?
opts: The dominoes fall up to the gap, and then the chain stops
quiz.why: The domino before the gap has nothing to hit. A chain of causes stops where a link is missing.

quiz.p: Why can a gap be too wide for a domino chain?
opts: The falling domino cannot reach the next one high enough to tip it
quiz.why: A domino can only tip the next one if it hits it well above the bottom. If the gap is as wide as the domino is tall, it just reaches the bottom.

quiz.p: A coin slides into a line of touching coins. What do the coins in the middle do?
opts: They fly off in all directions
They hardly move, but pass the push on
quiz.why: The middle coins pass the push to the next coin and stay almost still. Only the last coin slides away.

quiz.p: Two coins slide together into a line of touching coins. What usually happens at the far end?
quiz.why: Usually the same number of coins leaves the far end as came in. Two in, two out.

quiz.p: Dry chana are put in water at night. When can we see the effect?
quiz.why: The chana soak up water slowly, so they become big only after many hours. Some effects come long after their cause.

quiz.p: Which of these effects takes years to come?
opts: A clang from a dropped spoon
A mango tree growing from a seed
A curtain moving in the fan's wind
quiz.why: A seed takes years to grow into a tree. The clang and the moving curtain happen in a moment.

quiz.p: Every morning a rooster crows, and then the Sun rises. What is true?
opts: The rooster makes the Sun rise
The rooster crows because morning is coming
The Sun makes the rooster quiet
quiz.why: The Sun rises even when the rooster is quiet. Coming first does not make something the cause.

quiz.p: Long ago, many people thought maggots grew by themselves out of rotting meat. What did Francesco Redi's covered jars show?
opts: Maggots come from eggs that flies lay
Meat turns into maggots when it gets old
quiz.why: No maggots grew where flies could not reach the meat. The real cause was the flies' eggs.

applications: Doctors look for the cause of an illness, such as a germ or a lack of a vitamin, so they can treat the cause and not only the effects.
Weather scientists at the India Meteorological Department follow chains of causes, from warm seas to winds to clouds, to say when the monsoon will reach Kerala.
Engineers who build lifts, bridges and trains test what would happen if one part broke, so one broken link does not stop or harm everything.
Mechanics and electricians follow a chain back, step by step, to find which part stopped a scooter or a fan from working.
Farmers know that what they do now, such as adding compost to the soil, has effects on the crop months later.

open_questions.why_open: For big things, we can almost always find causes. But some tiny atoms break apart at moments nobody can predict or explain. Physicists still argue whether there is any cause for when that happens.

open_questions.q: Where does a chain of causes begin?
open_questions.why_open: If you follow causes back, each one has a cause before it. Scientists trace chains back to the beginning of the universe, but nobody knows what, if anything, came before that.

open_questions.q: When you choose to do something, what caused your choice?
open_questions.why_open: Your choices have causes, such as what you saw, what you felt and what you remember. Scientists and thinkers still argue about how free our choices are.

maths.problem: Kavya stood 10 dominoes in a line and took out the fifth one. When she pushed the first, 4 fell. How many dominoes were still standing?
maths.explain: She took 1 domino out, so 9 were in the line. 4 fell. 9 take away 4 is 5. So 5 stayed standing after the gap.
maths.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.
maths.why_maths: Counting what fell and what stood tells you exactly where the chain stopped.

maths.problem: Each of Kavya's dominoes is 5 centimetres tall. A gap must be less than one domino's height for the chain to work. Which of these gaps will work: 2 centimetres, 4 centimetres or 6 centimetres?
maths.explain: 2 and 4 are both less than 5, so the falling domino can reach the next one. 6 is more than 5, so the falling domino lies flat before it reaches the next one.
maths.context: This question is about the domino gap test. You stood ten dominoes in a line, pushed the first one, and counted how many fell with three different gaps.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each gap with the height of a domino lets you predict which line will fall before you even try.

maths.problem: In the morning, 10 soaked chana made a line 12 centimetres long. About how long would a line of 20 soaked chana be?
maths.explain: 20 chana is two lots of 10. Each lot of 10 makes about 12 centimetres. 12 and 12 make 24.
maths.context: This question is about soaking chana. You measured a line of ten dry chana at night, soaked them, and measured them again in the morning.
maths.why_maths: Thinking in equal groups lets you predict a longer line without lining up every chana.

maths.problem: In Pass the Push, a line of 4 people passed the pat to the front in about 2 seconds. If 8 people stand in the line, about how long will it take?
maths.explain: 8 people is twice as many as 4. Each person needs about the same moment to feel the pat and pass it on. So it takes about twice as long: 2 and 2 make 4 seconds. Your real time may be a little more or less.
maths.context: This question is about the Pass the Push game. Players stood in a line, and each one patted the next person's shoulder only after feeling a pat.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern, twice the people and twice the time, lets you predict how long a longer chain will take.

roots.context: We have knocked down dominoes, sent a push through a line of coins and watched chana swell overnight. Now we ask what chains of causes tell us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In your domino line, your finger pushed only the first domino. Yet the last one fell too, because each domino pushed the next. When one gap was too wide, the push stopped there, and the rest stayed standing. So one small push can reach far away, as long as every link passes it on.
deep_truth.habit: We usually name one cause for an effect, such as 'my finger knocked them down' or 'the wind did it'. The domino test shows that every link in between is a cause too, and taking away any one of them stops the effect.
deep_truth.evidence: In the domino gap test, one gentle push knocked down all ten dominoes when the gaps were small. With the widest gap, or with one domino taken out, the chain stopped at that spot and the rest stayed standing.

three.who_am_i: You are the effect of a very long chain: your parents and grandparents, the food you have eaten and the air you have breathed. And everything you do starts new chains.
three.what_is_life: Living beings take in causes and pass them on. A chana seed drinks water and swells. An ant finds sugar and tells the others.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of chains of causes that cross each other everywhere. A coconut falling in the night can reach all the way to a new friendship.

roots.thread: Before the push, the line of dominoes stood still, ready to fall. One push, one single action, became ten falls, one after another. In the same way, one coconut falling became a line of stopped cars, a late van and a new friend. One cause keeps becoming many effects. Everything is conscious, the dominoes and the coins too, each one taking in the push and passing it on in their own way. Many scientists disagree, and say only living beings with brains are aware.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 12.21, in the Pali Canon, the oldest written collection of the Buddha's teachings
teachings.teaching: When this is, that is. When this arises, that arises. When this is not, that is not. When this stops, that stops.
teachings.link: When the fifth domino was there, the push went on. When it was taken away, the push stopped there. Each domino falls only because the one before it does.

teachings.source: Samkhya Karika, verse 9, by Ishvarakrishna, written more than 1,500 years ago
teachings.teaching: An effect comes only from a cause that is able to make it. Not everything can come from everything. Teachers explaining this verse say that oil comes from sesame seeds, never from sand.
teachings.link: Francesco Redi showed that maggots come only from fly eggs, never from the meat by itself. Chana swell only when there is water for them to drink.

science.text: When a domino or a coin hits the next one, it passes on some of its energy. That is how one push can travel down a whole line. A scientist called Lorne Whitehead showed in 1983 that a domino can knock over one about one and a half times bigger.
Some tiny atoms break apart at moments nobody can predict. Physicists still argue whether anything at all causes the exact moment.

other_view.who: David Hume, a Scottish thinker, in his book An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, 1748
other_view.view: Hume said we never actually see a cause making an effect happen. We only see one thing, and then another thing, again and again. Because we are used to it, we expect the second whenever we see the first. So 'cause' may be partly a habit of our minds.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. Empty matchboxes stood on their short end are about 5 centimetres tall and topple well on a tiled floor with the fan off. A one-finger gap and a half-height gap both let all ten fall. With a gap as wide as the box is tall, the first box lies flat with its top just touching the foot of the next, so the chain stops at once. Taking out one box stops the chain at the hole. Ten same coins on a carrom board or a smooth table pass a push to the last coin, and the middle coins barely shift. Ten dry chana make a line of about 7 to 8 centimetres, and after a night in water the line is clearly longer.
